newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study highlights health of poor, old in HMOs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study highlights health of poor, old in HMOs.

text.p: Chronically ill poor and elderly people were far more likely to suffer declines in health when treated in health maintenance organisations than in fee-for-service systems, a study released on Tuesday found.

For the average patient, physical and mental health outcomes did not differ between health maintenance organisations (HMOs) and fee-for-service (FFS) systems, a research team led by John Ware, of the New England Medical Centre in Boston, Mass., found.
But outcomes did differ for the poor and the elderly who were chronically ill.
Under a traditional fee-for-service plan, the insurance carrier picks up part of the insured person's health care costs, after a deductible, and the patient pays the rest.
HMOs provide health care through a network of doctors and hospitals and patients pay a fixed co-payment for services.
Enrollments in HMOs have increased nearly 10-fold since 1976, but until this study little was known about the health outcomes of the elderly and poor in HMOs, the researchers said.

The researchers studied 2,235 patients in Boston, Chicago and Los Angeles from 1986 to 1990. The patients, whose ages ranged from 18 to 97, suffered from chronic illnesses including hypertension, non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, recent acute myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure and depressive disorder.
The findings were published in The Journal of the American Medical Association and announced at the association's science reporters conference in San Francisco.

The study found that among patients aged 65 and older treated under Medicare -- a federal health insurance programme for the elderly -- declines in physical health over a four-year period were about twice as common in HMOs as in FFS plans (54 percent compared to 28 percent).
Patients in the low-income group also had worse physical outcomes in HMOs than in FFS plans, they said. The results were similar for each of the three study sites.
"Patients who were elderly and poor were more than twice as likely to decline in health in an HMO than in an FFS plan (68 percent ... in an HMO versus 27 percent for FFS)," the researchers found.

"These results indicate that all HMOs are not created equal," Ware said. "That is why a 'consumer report' on quality of care is needed for each health plan -- HMO and fee-for- service -- and not just their price," he said.

The researchers said their results sent a cautionary message to policy-makers who expect overall experiences to date with HMOs to apply equally to subgroups such as Medicare beneficiaries or the poor.
"Current health care plans should carefully monitor the health outcomes of these vulnerable subgroups," they said.
